Analysis by Richard Cowan

One of the benefits of the Internet that I particularly appreciate is how it allows us to

assemble facts from around the world and create context much more easily than was ever

possible before.

Here are a few stories that that demonstrate this point.

First, Montana's Department of Corrections wants to prohibit anyone on parole or

probation from using medical marijuana, which they would be able to do as a result of the

state’s 2004 initiative. It is not uncommon for “law enforcement” to decide that a state’s

medical marijuana laws really don’t apply in “their” area.

Of course, the American Civil Liberties Union of Montana is opposing the move as are

local marijuana reform activists. I expect the parole board to do whatever it wants and the

people of Montana will have to pay for the cost of putting more people in prison and for the

litigation that will result.

The parole board says that alcohol and “drug” use causes higher recidivism rates, which

may be true, but is entirely irrelevant. Would it be alright if prisoners used prescribed

Valium, like the young man who massacred shoppers at a mall last month?

The second story was about dog lover and former football star Michael Vick. He is joining

a “prison-monitored drug rehabilitation program” in Leavenworth, Kansas.

It seems that Vick may be “addicted to marijuana”, and if he manages to stay clean and say

all the right things to show that he has been reeducated and rehabilitated, etc., he may be

able to get out of prison much sooner than expected.

Vick had failed a “drug test” for marijuana after pleading guilty to the dog fighting

charges, and this caused the judge to give him a longer sentence. Heretofore, I had not been

aware of a connection between dog fighting and marijuana use, but I am sure when Vick

has overcome his addiction, he will join PETA.

Translation: Vick has a very good lawyer, who knows how to play the system.

So… if you are seriously ill in Montana, you can be sent back to prison for using medical

marijuana, but if you claim to be addicted to marijuana and go through rehab you can get

out of prison.

Whatever!

But consider the magnitude of the insanity. There are almost 5 million Americans on either

probation or parole and subject to “drug testing” at any time.There are also more people are behind bars in the United States than in any other country.

China ranks second with 1.5 million prisoners, followed by Russia with 870,000.

The U.S. incarceration rate of 737 per 100,000 people is the highest, followed by 611 in

Russia. In contrast, the incarceration rates in many Western industrial nations range

around 100 per 100,000 people.

The “leader of the free world” has 5 percent of the world's population and 25 percent of the

world's prisoners

“Drug” offenders account directly for about 2 million of the 7 million in prison, on

probation or parole, but many more indirectly.

(The numbers are from the annual report from the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice

Statistics.)

In March of 2005, the Las Vegas Mercury published an article by Randall G. Shelden , a

criminal justice professor at UNLV, which offered a very interesting insight into how “drug

testing” has contributed to the boom in the prison business.

Excerpt:

“In some states as many as 40 percent of prison admissions have been probation or parole

violators. In Michigan, for instance, a recent study found that the growth in prison

admissions from 1990 to 1997 was 41 percent for parole violators and 33 percent for probation

violators.

In California, the proportion entering prison last year for parole violations was just under 70

percent….

A researcher in California once saw a sign in the office of the head of a parole office that

said: ‘Trail 'em, surveil 'em, nail 'em, jail 'em.’ An exhaustive study of the prison and parole

system arrived at the conclusion that the rise in parole violations resulting in a prison sentence

‘is attributable in large part to dramatic changes in the nature of parole supervision and the

imposition of increasingly more severe conditions of supervision on parolees.’”

Recently, an Op-ed in the LA Times complained about “severe overcrowding in the state's

prisons -- as high as 200% of capacity -- that has produced conditions of such ‘extreme peril’

for prisoners and guards that Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger was forced to declare a

systemwide state of emergency in 2006. Since 2003, the inmate population has grown 8%, to

about 173,000. But the budget of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation has

skyrocketed 79%, to $8.5 billion, becoming the fastest-growing category in the state budget

and a factor in opening up a $14-billion budget deficit.

The get-tough-on-crime laws also have helped create a crisis in California's prison healthcare

system, where spending has risen to $1.9 billion a year, up 263% since 2000… The system

became so understaffed and dysfunctional that a federal judge ruled that it was causing at

least one avoidable death a week through sheer neglect and ineptitude. He has seized theentire prison medical system and placed it under his direct supervision.”

In fact, prisons are becoming public health and safety threats around the world. Recently

an Op-ed in the Guardian made a very sad observation:

“One of the perversities of prison life is that you get the same punishment for having evidence

of any drug found in your urine. However, due to the time it takes to metabolise the chemicals,

cannabis remains in your system far longer than heroin, so a number of young people go into

prison as cannabis users and come out as heroin addicts. There are tales told of low security

prisons where drugs are smuggled out rather than in because they are less available and

thereby attract a better price in the nearest town than in the prison itself.

People in prison for the first time gain an induction into criminal life and make criminal

contacts. People become drug addicts in prison. Some people get raped and dehumanised in

prison. Some people commit suicide in prison.”

Some civilizations do the same.
